facts.statement: The genus Plioplatecarpus includes the type species P. marshi described by Dollo in 1882, along with other species such as P. depressus, P. primaevus, P. houzeaui, and P. peckensis.
facts.quote: P. marshi Dollo, 1882 (type) P. depressus (Cope, 1869) P. primaevus Russell, 1967 P. houzeaui (Dollo, 1889) P. peckensis Cuthbertson and Holmes, 2015

facts.statement: The genus Oterognathus is a synonym of Plioplatecarpus.
Plioplatecarpus belongs to the subfamily Plioplatecarpinae.
Phosphorosaurus is another synonym of the genus Plioplatecarpus.
Plioplatecarpus lived during the late Cretaceous period, approximately 82 to 68 million years ago.
facts.quote: Like all mosasaurs, it lived in the late Cretaceous period, about 82-68 million years ago.

facts.statement: Plioplatecarpus lived in the Upper Cretaceous, about 83.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Como todos los mosasaurios, vivió en el Cretácico Superior, hace cerca de 83.5 millones de años.

facts.statement: The fossil record for Plioplatecarpus spans from the Cenomanian to the Danian stages, between 100.5 and 61.66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Danian (100.5 to 61.66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Plioplatecarpus was first discovered in Europe by paleontologist Louis Dollo in 1882.
facts.quote: It was first found in Europe by paleontologist Louis Dollo (P. marshi), in 1882.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope found a specimen in North America in 1869 that was initially identified as Mosasaurus but was later reclassified as Plioplatecarpus in 1870.
facts.quote: In North America, Edward Drinker Cope found another mosasaur in 1869, but had identified it as Mosasaurus. It would later be reclassified as Plioplatecarpus, as would Cope's Liodon, in 1870.

facts.statement: In North America, Edward Drinker Cope identified a mosasaur found in 1869 as Mosasaurus, which was later reclassified as Plioplatecarpus in 1870.
facts.quote: En Norteamérica, Edward Drinker Cope encontró otro mosasaurio en 1869, pero lo había identificado como Mosasaurus. Sería reclasificado más adelante como Plioplatecarpus, en cambio del género Liodon, en 1870.

facts.statement: Fossils of Plioplatecarpus have been found in the Pierre Shale of Kansas, Demopolis Chalk of Alabama, Mississippi, North Dakota, South Dakota, Canada, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Wyoming.
facts.quote: Pliopltecarpus se ha encontrado en la Pizarra Pierre de Kansas, en la tiza de Demopolis de Alabama, y también en Misisipi, Dakota del Norte, Dakota del Sur, Canadá, Suecia, los Países Bajos, y, más recientemente en, Wyoming.

facts.statement: Plioplatecarpus was a medium-sized mosasaur, with P. marshi reaching 5.5 meters in length and P. houzeaui measuring between 5 and 6 meters.
facts.quote: Plioplatecarpus was a medium-sized mosasaur, with P. marshi measuring 5.5 m long and P. houzeaui measuring 5 - 6 m long.

facts.statement: Plioplatecarpus had proportionally larger eyes than many other mosasaur genera, despite having a relatively short skull.
facts.quote: Los ojos de Plioplatecarpus son proporcionalmente más grandes que los de muchos otros mosasaurios, aunque el cráneo sea relativamente corto.

facts.statement: Plioplatecarpus had fewer teeth than most mosasaurs, with only about 12 or fewer, which were large and curved.
facts.quote: Tiene menos dientes que la mayoría de los mosasaurios (solamente cerca de 12, o menos), pero eran grandes y curvos.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the larger eyes of Plioplatecarpus may be an adaptation to low-light conditions in deeper water.
facts.quote: The larger eyes may be an adaptation to low light conditions like those found in deeper water.

facts.statement: The greatly recurved teeth of Plioplatecarpus suggest it hunted relatively small prey that it could grasp precisely.
facts.quote: It has fewer teeth than most mosasaurs, but they are greatly recurved. This suggests that Plioplatecarpus would have hunted relatively small prey that it could grab very precisely.

facts.statement: The wide distribution of fossils in North America and Europe suggests Plioplatecarpus was an open ocean predator.
facts.quote: The broad distribution of fossil remains in both North America and Europe suggest that it would have been an open ocean predator.

facts.statement: A 1999 study described a specimen from a non-marine deposit, suggesting Plioplatecarpus might have entered freshwater and estuarine habitats.
facts.quote: In 1999, Holmes and colleagues described an incomplete specimen of Plioplatecarpus from an early Maastrichtian non-marine deposit, suggesting that this genus might have entered freshwater and estuarine habitats.

rejected.statement: It is debated whether the freshwater specimen of Plioplatecarpus represents a random occurrence or evidence that mosasaurs lived in both marine and freshwater environments.
rejected.quote: While the describers of Pannoniasaurus considered this specimen as a random occurrence in a freshwater environment, Taylor and colleagues in 2021 suggested that this specimen and Pannoniasaurus directly support that mosasaurs lived in both marine and freshwater habitats.
rejected.reason: statement copies the source wording: 'that mosasaurs lived in both marine and freshwater'
